newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: OECD, World Bank warn about private sector abuse.
newsitem.headline: OECD, World Bank warn about private sector abuse.

text.p: The World Bank and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) on Monday hailed the rapid growth ot the private sector in Latin America and other emerging markets but warned against firms becoming too dominant or monopolistic.
"We will emphasize rules for restrictive agreements about abuse of dominant economic groups and mergers control," Shyam Khemani, the World Bank's chief industrial economist told Reuters.

"These rules must be harmonized in a deeper degree and we have to work towards their convergence," he said on the opening day of a three-day emerging market forum on competition policy co-sponsored by the World Bank, the OECD and the Argentine government.

Rainer Geiger, OECD's Deputy Director for Financial, Fiscal and Enterprise Affairs told the meeting: "Private sector has developed rapidly. Trade among Latin American countries, and between the region and the rest of the world has a great role in that growth."
But he warned it was important "to prevent corporations from rising new barriers against trade by means of restrictive commercial practices."

The forum will discuss issues relating to cartels, including ways to determine if a dominant group has engaged in abusive monopolistic practices. It will also address issues such a mergers and acquisitions and their links with privatization and investment policies.
"The greastest challenge of this workshop is to define conditions for an effective competition policy," Geiger said.
Khemani said the conference aims to foster greater cooperation and harmonization of competition policies.
"This is a forum by which non-OECD countries can benefit from the advice of international experts as theses countries are trying to formulate economic policies in specific areas," he added.

Competition policy has a role to play in prompting market access, adjustment and adaptability of domestic economics by preventing restrictive private business practices as governments are bringing down tariff and non-tariff barriers, he said.

Argentina's secretary for International Economic Relations Jorge Campbell said his country was updating its competition legislation dating from 1980 to take into account the trade liberalization introduced in the 1990s.
In particular, Argentina would seek to make it compatible with Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, its partners in the Mercosur customs union, he said.
